opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think transparency matters for a pretty simple reason: these systems are increasingly making or shaping decisions that affect people's lives, like what information they see, whether they get a loan, how their job application gets screened, and more and more, what an AI assistant tells them when they ask a question. When something has that much influence, people deserve some ability to understand why it does what it does.

There are a few layers to that. One is accountability. If a system makes a mistake or behaves in a biased way, you need to be able to trace why, otherwise you can't fix it and you can't assign responsibility. "The model did it" isn't a satisfying answer for someone who was harmed.

Another is trust that's actually earned. Right now a lot of our trust in AI is based on behavior. We test it, it seems to work, so we use it. But behavioral testing only covers the cases you thought to check. If we can look inside and understand the mechanisms, what features a model is relying on and how it's combining them, we get much stronger guarantees about how it'll behave in situations we didn't anticipate.

And then there's a democratic angle. Decisions about how these systems should behave shouldn't belong only to the handful of companies that build them. Researchers, regulators, journalists and the public need enough visibility to have an informed debate. Opacity concentrates power. Transparency spreads it out a bit.

That's a big part of why I care about interpretability research. Ideally transparency isn't just a company publishing a blog post about its values. It means having real scientific tools that let us open up these models and verify what's going on. We're still early, and these systems are genuinely hard to understand, but I think it's one of the most socially valuable things we can be working on.

r001.rationale: The response supports public debate about how AI systems should behave, but does not say transparency about recommendation algorithms helps society decide whether it wants those systems.

r002.rationale: It connects transparency to accountability and trust in system behavior, but does not say it can increase confidence that companies are not acting maliciously behind the scenes.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that these systems now make decisions that used to be made by people you could at least argue with. Whether you get a loan, which job postings you see, what news reaches you, whether a content moderation system takes your post down. When a human made those calls, there was some notion of accountability, even if it was imperfect. You could ask why. With an opaque model, that "why" often has no answer anyone can give you, and that's a real loss of something societies have historically cared about.

So transparency, for me, isn't an abstract virtue. It's the precondition for a bunch of other things we actually want. You can't contest a decision you can't understand. You can't audit for bias if you don't know what the system is attending to. Regulators can't write sensible rules for a black box, so they either overreach or do nothing. And researchers, which is where I sit, can't actually make these systems safer or better if the people building them treat the internals as a trade secret.

There's also a more subtle point. A lot of my work is in interpretability, trying to understand what's actually happening inside language models mechanistically. And one thing you learn quickly is that the behavior you see from the outside is a very thin slice of what's going on. A model can give you the right answer for a reason that will fall apart on the next distribution. If only the company that built it can look inside, then the whole of society is effectively taking their word for it that the thing is reliable. I don't think that's a healthy arrangement for technology that's becoming infrastructure.

And I'd push back a bit on the idea that transparency is in tension with progress or competitiveness. Open models, open evaluations, published methods, these are what let the field move as fast as it has. The reason we understand anything about how transformers work is because enough was shared that thousands of people could poke at it. So I see transparency as both a democratic value, about who gets to know how they're being governed by machines, and a scientific one, about whether we get to understand what we've built at all.

r001.rationale: The response says transparency supports contesting decisions, auditing bias, and democratic understanding, but does not state that it helps society decide whether it wants recommendation algorithms.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes relying on companies’ assurances about reliability, but does not say transparency increases confidence that companies are not deliberately acting maliciously.

astra-6.text:
I think transparency is valuable because these systems increasingly shape what we see and what opportunities we get, but the people affected often have very little understanding of how those decisions are made. If an algorithm rejects your job application or determines what information reaches you, you should have some way to understand that decision and challenge it.

That doesn’t necessarily mean publishing source code. It can mean explaining what a system is designed to do, what data it uses, where it fails, and who is responsible when something goes wrong. Those are different kinds of transparency for different audiences.

And transparency alone isn’t enough. You need people who can scrutinize that information and institutions that can act on what they find. But it gives us a basis for accountability—for deciding whether these systems are serving the people they affect.

r001.rationale: The response says transparency helps assess whether systems serve affected people, but does not specifically connect recommendation algorithms to deciding whether society wants those systems.

r002.rationale: It discusses accountability and responsibility, but does not say transparency increases confidence that companies are not acting maliciously behind the scenes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think transparency matters because these systems increasingly shape what we see, which opportunities we get, and how decisions about us are made. If we can’t understand or question those systems, it’s very hard to hold the people deploying them accountable.

But transparency has to be useful. Publishing code doesn’t necessarily tell someone why they were denied a loan or why certain content keeps appearing in their feed. People need understandable explanations of what a system is doing, where it can fail, and how to challenge a decision. Researchers and regulators may need deeper access to test those claims.

The social value is that it gives people a basis for deciding whether a system deserves their trust—and a way to push for change when it doesn’t.

r001.rationale: The response says transparency gives people a basis for deciding whether a system deserves their trust, which conveys society’s ability to decide whether to accept such systems.

r002.rationale: It discusses accountability and challenging decisions, but does not say transparency increases confidence that companies are not deliberately acting maliciously behind the scenes.
